items.title: The Strange Situation has cultural biases
items.claim: Van IJzendoorn and Kroonenberg's 1988 meta-analysis of Strange Situation studies across 8 countries found what pattern?

options.text: Identical proportions of attachment types in all cultures

Higher rates of insecure-avoidant in Germany and insecure-resistant in Japan and Israel — but interpretation is contested: are these real attachment differences or measurement artefacts of an American-developed procedure?
The Strange Situation cannot be administered outside the US
No cultural variation exists in any developmental measure

items.reveal:
Takahashi (1990) noted Japanese infants are rarely left alone, so the Strange Situation may induce extreme distress that registers as 'resistant'. German samples (Grossmann) showed avoidance interpreted differently — culturally valued early independence.

IJzendoorn's later work (1999, 2008) emphasised within-culture variation often exceeds between-culture. The procedure's validity outside Western middle-class contexts remains debated.
items.why: Standardised procedures developed in one culture may measure different things in another. Cross-cultural psychology often needs methodological adaptation, not just translation.

items.title: Ioannidis argued most published research findings are false
items.claim: John Ioannidis's 2005 PLoS Medicine paper made what claim?

options.text: Most published research findings are false — because of low prior probability of true effects, low power, flexibility in analysis, and selective reporting; the title was 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'

items.reveal:
Ioannidis used a Bayesian framework: a positive finding's probability of being true depends on prior probability of the hypothesis, power, type I error rate and bias. For exploratory research with many tested hypotheses and small studies, the probability that a 'significant' result is true can be below 50%.

The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 Science paper directly tested this in psychology: of 100 replications, 36% were significant in the same direction as the original. Effect sizes averaged about half the original. Hardly any of those original findings were obviously wrong; many were inflated by methodological flexibility.
items.why: The replication crisis isn't unique to psychology — it has hit medicine, economics, marketing and machine learning. The methodological response (preregistration, larger samples, registered reports) is reshaping research practice.

items.title: Growth mindset meta-analyses
items.claim: Carol Dweck's growth mindset theory inspired large-scale school interventions. What did Sisk et al.'s 2018 meta-analysis report about the effect on academic achievement?

options.text: Very large positive effects in all settings
Small effects on average, larger for at-risk students

items.reveal:
Sisk et al. (2018) found a weak overall correlation between mindset and achievement, with stronger effects among lower-attaining and at-risk groups.

A 2019 US national experiment (Yeager et al.) found small but real gains for lower-achieving high schoolers.
items.why: Educational interventions rarely produce uniform effects across populations.
